So behind divider 2.

DR DEWI EVANS (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Could you please state your full name, Dr Evans?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Dewi Richard Evans.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. You are, I understand, a consultant paediatrician?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I am.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Could you please inform the jury when you first qualified medically?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I qualified from the Welsh National School of Medicine in 1971 and I carried out my first paediatric post 18 months later, so my paediatric junior training took place in Swansea, initially, and then in Cardiff and in Liverpool. Each phase of my training involved specific training, working in a neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Having passed through the various stages of training, could you confirm that you later became a National Health Service clinical consultant paediatrician?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I was appointed consultant paediatrician in Swansea in 1980. The most significant part of my brief, I think, was the development of newborn services for babies, particularly developing intensive care services for babies, which we did from scratch, really.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: How would you define your role in the development of those neonatal intensive care services in South Wales?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Swansea was one of the bigger units in South Wales and so we covered the area extending throughout the whole of South-west Wales over time. Initially, it was very much a matter of getting on with it, trying to get good equipment, getting the nursing and medical colleagues up to speed with regard to baby care. We've heard already about levels of intensive care, so we dealt with all the babies who were really sick and needing life support, in other words, requiring periods of ventilation for days, sometimes weeks. So therefore we developed all of those services during the 1980s and 1990s in Swansea and the only babies we did not deal with were those that required cardiac surgery and babies who required surgery, general surgery. So they were transferred to Cardiff or Bristol.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But all the tiny babies who require intensive care were under my care and the care of my colleagues in Swansea from 1980 onwards.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll return to aspects of your clinical experience in due course.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Could I just ask you to pause there?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Would you like to sit down? I think in fact we would like you to sit down for the purposes of the camera.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Is that all right? I think it'll be easier as well for you. The important thing is you have, if I may say so, a good strong voice, so that will carry across to the jury. It will be more comfortable for you to sit down, thank you, and helpful to us, apparently.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm obliged.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Evans, could you confirm that you are a fellow of the Royal College of Physicians?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I am.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: A fellow of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I am.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you have obtained a diploma in obstetrics from the Royal College of Obstetrics and Gynaecology?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So the jury understand your role in these proceedings, you've never been employed in the Countess of Chester Hospital?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: At no point you have been responsible for providing medical care or attention to any of the babies that we are to consider, in particular, in these proceedings?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: None at all.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Before I took you back to your qualifications, you were explaining to the jury some of your contribution to the development of neonatal care and the establishment of services in South Wales and you were, I anticipate, touching upon the developments that you observed during your long period as a consultant. And in summary, how would you characterise the evolution of the service under your supervision?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I think my generation were responsible, really, for the development, for the evolving of neonatal care in the UK. In the 1970s, babies who were small and ill died. There was very little care available for them, we did not have the expertise,
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: we did not have the monitoring, we did not have the equipment, so therefore it was very much an essential and important part of our generation that we provided good services, you know, for these ill babies.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So a lot of my experience was based not on reading books or finding out what was happening in other places, but very much hands-on, in other words you were there, you had a sick baby in an incubator, you'd place this baby on ventilatory support, the monitoring was nothing as good as it is now, and therefore very much of it was touch-and-go, really. It could be quite fraught because there were demands, other demands on children's services, but those of us who were really very passionate about these babies would go to places to get money to buy equipment and give stories in the press whenever one of our ill babies went home. In other words, just to get the publicity to get everybody involved with baby care.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I became involved with an organisation called Bliss because they were very supportive, collecting money for sick babies. So this was it in the 1980s.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Then in 1990, in Swansea, we built -- the health board built a brand new children's department, which included a brand new neonatal unit, which I helped design. So life became a bit easier because we had more space. By that time we had some fantastic -- well, we had some superb nursing staff who were excellent, and also by that time there were far, far more junior doctors who were developing an interest in baby care and therefore things took off from the 1990s.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. How did that hands-on approach that you've mentioned, how did that evolve in this period?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, babies arrived in the neonatal unit in all sorts of conditions. The most common problem were problems associated with prematurity and therefore one had to see them through, quite often, the first few days of life.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now, this meant giving oxygen. If giving oxygen was insufficient, one needed to give treatment called CPAP, continuous positive airway pressure, which has saved thousands of lives, I think, over the last few decades.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If they did not respond to treatment with CPAP they required what we called intubation, in other words you are to pass a breathing tube into the lungs and place them on ventilatory support. In other words, put them on a breathing machine. And the initial breathing machines were, I suppose, primitive compared to the ones we have now, but they worked, and in addition to giving babies ventilation support you also had to
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: give babies intravenous fluids because they were not well enough to absorb milk.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Therefore you had to -- well, give them cannulas, in other words pass a cannula, initially quite often into the umbilical vein and later into a vein in the hand or somewhere, wherever you could find a vein, really, to make sure that they were having adequate fluid, which on the whole consisted of glucose with electrolytes, in other words salt, and amino acids/protein. If you felt that they required intravenous nutrition for a long time, we've heard of total parenteral nutrition, TPN, then you'd have to work out a cocktail of nutrition that was appropriate to each baby.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So those developments continued during the 1980s and during the 1990s.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll return to the detail in due course, but how did the infrastructure of these departments evolve over those decades?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, all neonatal units are dedicated units, in other words they are responsible only for the care of newborn babies. So in other words, they're not responsible for infants of 3 months or whatever. So first of all they are neonatal units dedicated to small babies.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Usually, they're next door to the maternity unit, so therefore a baby can be transferred from the maternity unit to the neonatal unit promptly and quickly and they tend to be divided into sections. So you'd have the sickest baby in the intensive care area; I'll explain that in a bit more detail. Babies who were recovering would be in a high dependency area, and babies who were pretty well but too small to go home would be in the, if you like, the ordinary area, you know, what was called the growth area.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: In terms of the intensive care, this was where all the equipment would be concentrated mainly -- so by equipment, I'm talking ventilation -- sorry, let's start with an incubator. These babies were all nursed in an incubator to maintain their temperature. And then they'd be attached to various monitoring systems, okay?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Monitoring. And the monitoring would monitor heart rate, respiratory rate, later oxygen saturation, what we often call sats, oxygen saturation. Later, as things evolved, it became easier to monitor blood pressure in babies.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So those were the main features. So these babies were on continuous monitoring. You know, you'd look at a monitor, you
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: could see exactly what the heart rate was like and you'd know immediately if the oxygen saturation, you know, was falling or whatever.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Shortly, we'll show the jury a video of such equipment. But just returning to your experience and your clinical responsibilities, could you confirm that you were the clinical director, that is to say the head of department, of paediatrics and neonatology in Swansea --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- for the period 1992 to 1997 and the period 2004 to 2006?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. 2008, actually.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: 2008, forgive me.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Later on I took on being head of department that covered the maternity services as well, so you know -- so it was one organisation for one's maternity team and one's paediatric team.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Are you still a practising consultant paediatrician and neonatologist?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, no. I gave up my full-time clinical practice in 2009. I'd been in consultant practice for nearly 30 years, I thought that was enough, and that was my -- you know, that was the plan. I've done a few locums since then, short-term locums, but most of my input since then has been with preparing reports for the courts in relation to baby care and childcare. These reports -well, first of all, I've dealt with loads of court cases where there were allegations of clinical negligence involving small babies. So my first time as an independent medical witness was in 1988 and I've done that more or less up until about now, really.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I don't take on cases of clinical negligence anymore. Then increasingly, from the time I gave up my full-time clinical practice, I've become more involved in preparing reports for family courts where there are concerns regarding childcare or baby care and also for the Crown Court, where there are serious allegations of, you know, involving babies who are suspected of having died suspiciously or have had injuries.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And I've prepared a report both for police authorities, usually via the NCA, the National Crime Agency, and I've also prepared reports for law firms representing defendants.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Remind us of the times, please. So when did you begin appearing in civil and/or criminal courts as an expert witness?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Until now?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Until -- yes, until now, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Pausing there for a moment, members of the jury, and forgive me, Dr Evans, if we could go, please, behind divider 3.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: My Lord, whilst Dr Evans is still in court giving evidence, we're going to introduce some background agreed facts to give context to some of the evidence that Dr Evans will give in due course. So if I may, whilst Dr Evans remains with us, I'd like to introduce to the jury and read into the record some agreed facts.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. This is a legal direction in relation to agreed facts. They are what they say they are: facts that are agreed. In other words, the prosecution and the defence agree the facts that are set out here. So you can treat them as agreed evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The significance of the agreed facts, just as with any evidence and any findings that you make in relation to controversial evidence, evidence that isn't agreed, is entirely for you. You will decide the significance of any pieces of evidence or the insignificance of any piece of evidence and the way in which any piece of evidence assists you in your decision-making process.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: All right? But this is agreed evidence, so treat it as agreed evidence. You have it all written out here, you can refer to it as and when you need to if you need to at any stage, but it's obviously more helpful to have this than have a whole lot of evidence either called or read to you about these facts. It's a simple way of presenting agreed evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm grateful.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Members of the jury, you'll see this document is divided into sections and the first section is headed "The Cheshire and Mersey Neonatal Network". This is intended to inform you of the context of the events that you're going to consider.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So agreed fact number 1 -- and forgive me, Dr Evans, this is behind divider 3 if you care to follow.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Agreed fact number 1 reads:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Cheshire and Mersey Neonatal Network (sometimes referred to as the Mersey Cheshire Deanery) is a tiered network of hospitals.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: There are three tiers of hospitals designated to reflect how sick and/or premature a baby may be and the level of patient care required on a scale of 1 to 3. A level 3 unit is the most specialised and deals with the most difficult cases."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Sub-paragraph number 1:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "During the period June 2015 to June 2016, the Liverpool Women's Hospital (which is in Liverpool 8, close to the city centre) and Arrowe Park Hospital [which is in Upton, Birkenhead, Wirral] were designated as level 3 (also referred to as tertiary) neonatal intensive care units."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: And you'll see the abbreviated form of that title in brackets:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Those level 3 units routinely provided neonatal intensive care to babies with complex medical needs and babies of less than 27 weeks gestation."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Sub-paragraph 2:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "During the period June 2015 to June 2016, the Countess of Chester Hospital was designated as a level 2 unit and routinely provided care for babies of 27 weeks gestation and above and babies that required intensive care for up to 48 hours. Babies that required intensive care after 48 hours would normally be transferred to an intensive care unit (NICU) as described in the paragraph above. Babies of less than 27 weeks gestation born at or brought to the Countess of Chester Hospital would be stabilised and then transferred to a NICU on the same day."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Sub-paragraph number 3:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "During the period of June 2015 to June 2016, Leighton Hospital, Macclesfield Hospital, Ormskirk and District General Hospital, Warrington Hospital and Whiston Hospital were designated as level 1 units, sometimes referred to as local neonatal units."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Number 4:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Alder Hey Children's Hospital was the designated neonatal surgical unit for the network."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So that's, in very broad terms, the structure of the Cheshire and Mersey neonatal network of hospitals at the time that we are interested in. Dr Evans, could you confirm that this tiered approach is the NHS standard for England and Wales?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it is, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Now, moving on through this document briefly, you'll see that the next section, which is numbered currently number 3, but we'll just overwrite the number 2 there, please. Section 2, "The Countess of Chester Hospital". So we're now zooming in, as it were, on to the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So agreed fact number 2 pertaining to that hospital:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "During the period of June 2015 to June 2016" -- JUROR: Sorry, did you say section 2?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, there's a typing error. Mr Driver did say overwrite section 2.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I was trying to skate over the typo but I didn't get very far.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: It's a typo, so just write 2 over the 3 there. My documents are stapled together. It's very difficult to have stapled together documents in a lever arch file and it's not easy, actually, to remove staples. It's easier, frankly, to separate them. So I think we'll just pause for a moment to enable people to separate them. There are two ways of doing it, either taking it out of the file... The trouble is that once you take documents out then you've got to put them back in again and with lever arch files it's best to keep them altogether within their sections but separated individually as pages.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
So the content of section 2, the Countess of Chester Hospital. Agreed fact number 2 reads:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "During the period June 2015 to June 2016, the neonatal unit, the NNU [you'll become familiar with that abbreviation] of the Countess of Chester Hospital had four rooms, four nurseries: room 1 was the intensive care unit; room 2 was the high dependency unit; rooms 3 and 4 were special care units."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Agreed fact number 3:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Premature births or very ill babies were initially placed in room 1 and transferred to room 2 after a period of stability and then to rooms 3 and 4 to establish their feeds and spend more time with their parents with the intention of them going home."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Number 4:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "There were 16 designated cots on the unit, two ICU beds, one stabilisation and transfer bed, three high dependency beds (HDU beds) and 10 neonatal or special care (SC) beds."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Agreed fact number 5:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Additionally, there were four transitional care cots (TC cots) located on the postnatal ward where the baby would receive some neonatal nursing care and the mother would receive midwifery care in the same area."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Agreed fact number 6 deals with the access into and exit out of the hospital or the unit in the hospital, I should say:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Entry to the NNU at the Countess of Chester Hospital was controlled by locked doors. One was accessed from the public entrance side of the hospital, the other from the labour/maternity ward. From the outside, the door could be opened by use of an electronic pass or swipe card. From the inside, the door could be unlocked by pressing a button. Authorised staff at the NNU of the Countess of Chester Hospital were issued with individual electronic swipe cards, each with a unique reference number. Upon presentation of these cards to a door swipe reader, the secure door was opened and a record of location, time and date of that access was centrally recorded and stored on a database.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Only the use of a card was recorded. Corresponding data for the period May 2015 to July 2016 has been retrieved, although no records between July 2015 and October 2015 were available."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That retrieved data and records is exhibited and there is the exhibit reference number cited. So that was the system.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: But agreed fact 7 informs you:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "There were situations in which someone could enter the secure area and there would be no record. Examples of which are: 1, when someone, person A, opened the door with their pass and person B entered."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Two people entering at once with the use of one card.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Example 2: someone, person A, opened the door by pressing the button from the inside and allowing person B to enter."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So in that example, the entry of person B would not be recorded because he or she hasn't used their card, obviously.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "3. When people attended at the unit and pressed the entrance bell, the phone could operate the door and allow it to open and
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: buzz the individual into the unit and therefore individuals entering in this manner would not be recorded."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm sure you are all familiar with that sort of process.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Evans, could you confirm that you are familiar with those systems?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: They are commonplace?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, the norm these days.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Members of the jury, you've heard something about the systems in place at the Countess of Chester Hospital. Now we're going to play you, with the assistance of Mr Murphy, a walk-through of the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital. It's just short of 10 minutes long. This was recorded at a time when there were no patients or staff and there's commentary from a member of staff to explain to you the rooms and where the filming takes place.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Video played to the court)

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. In all contexts it's how you aspirate the stomach and aspirate the stomach simply means removing any fluid or milk or anything that is in the stomach.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You do it by connecting a syringe to the top end of the nasogastric tube and just sucking up on the syringe to see if any fluid or milk comes out. That's it.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Before we look at a demonstration video, we heard in the opening how it is protocol, can you confirm this, for a nurse to routinely seek to aspirate a neonate in these circumstances prior to each feed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Any baby who needs feeds via NG tube, and prior to the feed you would connect the syringe to the top end of the tube and aspirate the stomach, in other words empty the stomach. And the reason for doing this is that if there is a lot of residual milk in the stomach, then that baby is not well and is not -- and its digestive system is not working. So therefore, you have to have an empty stomach prior to the next feed.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. I wonder whether we could look at the NGT demonstration video, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Video played to the court)

Can we go back a few seconds just to make a point that may come in handy some time in the next few weeks? Just to make this point. If you look at the syringe, it's purple in colour and if you look at the top end of the nasogastric tube, that is also purple in colour. The reason for pointing this out is this: this kind of syringe can only be used in relation to oral or nasogastric feeds. You cannot connect a syringe of this type to an intravenous system and the importance of that is that you cannot inject milk into a vein by accident. So therefore, this colour coding is very important and has been around for some time.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: When you say it cannot be used for that purpose, is that because of the shape?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, the two connections are incompatible.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Video playing continued)

This is known as a gravity feed and the important thing is, you allow the milk to trickle through at its own rate, and that's quite important. You don't use the syringe to sort of force the milk through, you let it take its time.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Video playing continued)

Pausing there, Dr Evans, we saw the manual aspiration technique and then we've just been referred to free drainage. Can you explain to the jury the process by which free drainage achieves the required end?

Free drainage is very simple: you leave the nasogastric tube in, one end is in the stomach, and the other end is open and it's not covered, in other words it's an open end. And therefore if you get any air in the stomach for any reason, it can escape through the NG tube and that's it, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. I think we'd reached the end of the video, but let's press play in case there's something I've forgotten. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We've just dealt with the tube being used to take materials out of the baby. It's also used as part of the feeding process. Can we just think for a moment or two about what babies are fed with in the context of the unit. With reference to milk, we've also heard reference to EBM.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. EBM is expressed breast milk. Therefore this is milk expressed by the mother to give to the baby.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There's another term, DEBM, which is donor-expressed breast milk, which is milk from other mothers that is collected in what's often called a milk bank.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So in terms of which babies are fed by the nasogastric tube, most commonly babies who are premature. Premature babies have not acquired an effective sucking reflex, so they can't suck on a teat or on a nipple, and this does not develop until, you know, term, until around the time they should be born.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Therefore a baby who is, for instance, born 10 weeks early may require nasogastric feeds for many, many weeks.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The other type of baby that would require -- may require nasogastric feed is a baby who's sustained neurological damage, brain damage, affecting its sucking reflex and also its swallowing reflex, because if you can't suck and you can't swallow, you will choke if anybody gives you oral feeds. But the most common reason why babies are fed nasogastric feeds is to do with prematurity.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. You have dealt with breast milk, either from the baby's mother or from a donor. What about in circumstances where there isn't either any available or the baby is given some other feed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The other milk is formula feed. There are specialist milks designed for small babies and they tend to be higher in calories than the milk you buy in the chemist.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore they tend to have a calorie content on the whole of 80 calories per 100ml whereas ordinary milk is about 65 calories per 100ml. It's a higher calorie milk and there are a number of specialist milks available for prem babies.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And the jury heard earlier this week repeated reference to what Mr Johnson referred to as Babiven; is that such a formula?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Now, there are loads of makes. I'm not familiar -- there are a load of commercial makes. I'm not familiar with Babiven, but...
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. What about lipids? We heard about babies being given lipids. What are they?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lipid is fat, it's the medical term for fat. Naturally milk contains fat, contains lipid. But in this context, when one is talking about lipid, you're talking about intravenous lipid, which one requires in babies who are unable to take any nutrition orally. So for whatever reason, they cannot absorb milk, they cannot take milk or any nutrition orally and therefore you have to feed them intravenously, what we call TPN, total parenteral nutrition.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There are two bits usually to the TPN. The main one is a collection or cocktail of fluids that contains electrolytes, salt, and amino acids and a few additives, vitamins. So that is given intravenously, usually through a long line via a syringe pump. We can talk about the syringe pump another time.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Lipid has a far higher calorie content than the other solution and therefore that is usually given in a separate system
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: intravenously to up the -- to increase the calorific requirement of a baby to as normal a value as one can achieve.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm not going to read it out, but members of the jury, if you go back a page and look at page 14 you'll see a definition of lipids at the top of page 14 and examples of the content are set out there.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Are you content with the accuracy of that definition?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's fine.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Coming back to page 15 of the glossary, towards the bottom of the page there's a reference to necrotising enterocolitis, again something that was referred to repeatedly during the opening. Abbreviated for good reasons to NEC. In the business you call it "neck" do you?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We do, NEC, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Good. It is defined here as:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "A serious gastrointestinal disorder where a portion of the bowel becomes inflamed and that portion of the bowel may die."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Could you --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's a condition that affects mainly the small intestine. In other words, that's the part of the intestine immediately following the stomach. The small intestine is pretty long. There is still contention as to what causes NEC, but it's probably the result of a combination of poor perfusion, poor blood supply, to that part of the intestine. It maybe associated with infection. So you know, there are two things, but sometimes you can get it without being sure why.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The sicker the baby, the greater the risk of NEC.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That's the important thing. The early symptoms tend to be those of a bit of abdominal distension, maybe babies being irritable. More seriously you'll get blood in the poo, in the stool, and you also can get bile from the nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Bile aspirates?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Bile aspirates. So early diagnosis is crucial because the earlier the diagnosis and the earlier you can get treatment, the
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: more likely you are to arrest the development of the condition and then the baby will settle without the need for surgery. The treatment on the whole consists of a combination of antibiotics, including metronidazole, which is in this list, a combination of antibiotics and stopping oral feeds.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So you stop oral feeds, give antibiotics, maintain fluid intravenously, and hope that everything settles.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll stay with this definition a little longer because we're going to hear a lot of reference to NEC, we know, in the evidence. Alongside the hole punch we see a list of potential symptoms, some of which you've already referred to. If we go through them:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Feed intolerance, abdominal distension, abdominal pain, blood in the stool [you've told us about], vomiting bile aspirates."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It speaks for itself. It says "symptoms may include": do all of those always feature or do some of them feature sometimes and not others?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. The more serious the condition, the greater the number of symptoms. So this is why doctors usually, if they suspect NEC, you'll get in with treatment quickly.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So stop feeds, antibiotics. Even if you're not absolutely sure of the diagnosis, because it is better to treat early than to risk it. There's another entry there, by the way, with mural bowel gas. In serious cases, an X-ray of the abdomen will show abnormalities where you can see air within the intestine itself.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: As a symptom of NEC?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: As a symptom of NEC. That's a significant, serious sign, and the most serious sign of all is if you get perforation, in other words a rupture of the intestine, which causes peritonitis. And the mortality rate in that situation is pretty high because some of these babies are so ill they are not well enough to tolerate surgery. So if it's a perforation, they have to get to a surgical unit, and the surgeons will do their best to remove the damaged bowel and hope that the baby will recover.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And hence in simple language, it's asserted at the end of this definition that it is a serious gastrointestinal emergency?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It is.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Hence, as you said to us, if there's any symptoms of it, doctors assume the worst and treat for it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And treat promptly.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Moving topics, please. We also heard a lot of references to doctors observing rashes or skin discolouration, changes in the appearance of skin.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Without going to the specifics of any of the babies that we shall concentrate on, if we just in general terms deal with skin discolouration. At page 19 of the glossary, members of the jury, there is a general definition of a rash. In the simplest terms:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Any discolouration on the skin that is of a new onset."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And there within our definition is a whole host of varieties of rashes, "Descriptions include", and there they are listed.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We won't go into them one by one. Then in the final paragraph, there's reference to a purpuric rash, purpuric in this context meaning purple. What can you tell us about that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. The first loads of rashes, they reflect discolouration of the skin for whatever cause. And on the whole, if you press on the skin, the discolouration fades. The difference with a purpuric rash is that it's caused by the leakage of blood, blood spots, underneath the skin. So therefore if you press on the skin, the rash does not fade and it is usually a pretty worrying sign.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There are a number of causes. It's associated with sepsis or septicaemia and it's also associated with problems of blood clotting, coagulation problems.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Babies with a low platelet count develop purpura and of course the two conditions often go together. Babies who are severely ill with sepsis will often frequently have coagulation problems, in other words the blood is slow to clot. So a purpuric rash is a serious clinical problem.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll return to rashes and your study of any learning in this regard later. We'll move on.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: the bottom of the page, we've got "respiratory arrest", which of course we've dealt with in part already. We'll look at
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: a video now, please, RC1221, intubation. We could have looked at it with CPR, but we'll play it now.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: (Video played to the court)
Pausing there, on the animation we've just seen the process by which the clinician seeks to render the airway visible. What is it anatomically that is taking place there?

Right. It's easier to do this than to explain it. You pass the laryngoscope with your left hand, you push it forward to expose the vocal cards -- the vocal cords are at the top of the trachea. The trachea is at the front of the oesophagus. If you get it wrong the tube, instead of going into the trachea, will go into the oesophagus, you know, the back of the throat.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Therefore, you get the laryngoscope, put it forward a little bit, and then that exposes the vocal cords.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You then get the endotracheal tube, which you link to an introducer to stiffen it because endotracheal tubes are quite supple, soft. And the introducer is on the inside of the endotracheal tube and you pass the tube, the endotracheal tube through the vocal cords into the trachea and you make sure they go beyond the vocal cords but not too far, because if they go too far they go down into one lung, which is not a good idea.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Therefore once you know that the endotracheal tube is through the cords, you fix the tube, remove the laryngoscope, remove the introducer, and then you do the fixings as described there.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. So this is a necessary step in the provision of ventilatory support?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So moving on to types of support that the jury have heard reference to. If we go to page 6 of the glossary, you'll see a reference to CPAP.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The jury have also heard of BiPAP.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And also full ventilation.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Could you, in a sweep, describe those three for the jury, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: CPAP is the least invasive form of giving babies respiratory support. So you fix the system over the airways and that allows the mix of oxygen and air that the baby requires at a higher pressure than atmospheric pressure. And we heard earlier about pressures of 5, 5 centimetres of water. Therefore, a baby on CPAP would be placed on a pressure of about 5 or 6.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The purpose of this is that when the baby breathes out, the lungs don't collapse, because the baby's lungs at all times are under a slightly increased pressure to keep it up. Okay?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: BiPAP is the same but the pressure regulates, so it regulates from, say, between 12 and 6, so it's a more sophisticated method.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Then what's been described as full ventilation -- clinical notes will talk about IPPV, intermittent positive pressure ventilation, which you can only deliver in a baby where an endotracheal tube has been passed. This requires a very sophisticated ventilator, breathing machine, which you connect to the baby. You set the relevant pressures, so you need a higher pressure to inflate the lung, you require a lower pressure to stop the lung collapsing. You need a rate -- in other words a rate of 30 per minute or whatever and you set all of that up.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Then you ensure that the baby's chest is moving up and down and you can hear air or air -- well, gas going into the lungs. And hopefully, the baby will improve.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The first sign -- and the signs of improvement would be that the oxygen saturation will return, become normal, over 90, and the heart rate will settle, hopefully, and the respiratory rate is then controlled by the ventilator setting.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If the baby fights the ventilator, as we say, in other words breathes against the ventilator, then that baby will receive sedation, with a drug such as morphine, to settle him down. That that allows the baby to benefit most from the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What's the problem with the baby breathing against the ventilator or fighting the process?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right, good question. If the baby's fighting the ventilator, you wonder whether he requires ventilation in the first place. That's the first point. But if it means that -- it means that the ventilator is not coordinating with a baby's normal or baby's effort to breathe and therefore the baby does
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: not benefit from the additional support that the baby is getting. Because one thing we should emphasise here: most of the time, babies on ventilators are not paralysed, they're not paralysed. A patient having an operation in a theatre receives pancuronium, a paralysing drug, therefore the anaesthetist and the ventilator takes control completely.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We don't do this in babies. They're small, so usually, one can manage, can get away without paralysing the baby, simply by giving sedation.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Could you further define the distinction between sedation and paralysing the baby in this context?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Paralysing means the baby wouldn't be able to move at all, in other words all the muscles stop moving, therefore there is no movement whatsoever. Sedation means the baby is quieter, more relaxed, morphine has an effect, and so it's like having a baby asleep.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because if there's swelling in the throat, if there are secretions in the throat which could be blood or mucus, yes -so if the laryngoscope is in the wrong size or the wrong place, so there are -- if the intubator is insufficiently experienced — let's hope that's unlikely. But the commonest problem is poor view of the throat because of swelling around the surrounding area. That's probably the commonest technical problem.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And by "surrounding area" you mean around the cords?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Around the cords, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Is the epiglottis in that area?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The epiglottis is the back of the throat, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Moving to something different. Neonatology, Dr Evans, is a particular specialty within medicine and nursing, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you've explained to us that's focusing upon babies up to about 4 weeks in age?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is the definition of neonatology, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And that means that in neonatology, you are dealing with specifics for that particular group of patients, particular issues and the ways they present?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And just to explain, I know you can assist, neonates have, for example, specific anatomical or physiological features, don't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And obviously they tend to be smaller and less heavy, lower weight, than other patient groups?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And there will be particular items of equipment that might apply to neonates that might not apply with other patient groups?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And when it comes to interpreting the readings, for instance, looking at blood gas and the readings we get from that, that may be specific to neonates, mightn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It depends, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. And things like the vital signs, breathing or heart rate and things like that, as we've seen, are particular to neonates and dosing of drugs and what have you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And indeed, feeding them is different?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: A doctor who specialises, I'm talking about doctors at the moment in this area, is called a neonatologist?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now, when a doctor specialises in a particular area, she or he will, one anticipates, have training --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- that fits them for that area. They will work in an environment where they learn the skills and build them up in that area; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And they also gain experience and knowledge from doing the work itself --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- in a clinical setting?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: For those who aren't doctors, which certainly is me, to explain what you mean by the experience, clinical experience means the kind of daily exposure to patients and issues with patients that give the doctor a working knowledge of that area?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It also covers, doesn't it, things like discussions with colleagues day to day?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: A lot is learnt from the people alongside whom you work?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And then also if you are doing the work, you will see variations in the different conditions and patients, won't you —
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- over the years?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And sometimes the differences in conditions and how you approach them may be quite subtle, would you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, you take every item on its own merit, really.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's too general a point to be specific.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The more experience, the more exposure a doctor has had to a particular specialty, the greater his or her knowledge?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Hopefully, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And ability to interpret and deal with what they encounter?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The case we're dealing with and going to be dealing with for some months here, so far as we expect, revolves primarily around neonatology, doesn't it? You are not a consultant, this isn't to be rude, we'll go through your experience and specialty in a moment, but you are not a consultant neonatologist, are you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm a consultant paediatrician.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That's correct. You're a consultant paediatrician and you have had significant experience of neonatology?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Over 30 years, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And we'll come and have a look at that in a moment but I make it plain my questions are not intended to be discourteous or in any way minimise the extent of your knowledge, I make that quite plain, this isn't that, it's just to look at the extent of that, I hope that's clear, as you'll see.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The bulk of your experience in neonatology is via the unit that you'd set up in Swansea?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And that was during the 1980s into the 1990s?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And the 2000s.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And in 2004 to 2008?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, no, from 1980 until 2007/2008.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's the 1980s through to the 1990s when you were most heavily involved in that; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And the work you did as a neonatologist was done alongside other paediatric duties?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And so in that sense, you weren't someone who was working exclusively in neonatology?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We have the benefit of your CV, Dr Evans. Just to confirm with you, the way it's described, just over the period 1980 to 2009, and you've got a entry -- it's under "Clinical experience and interests":
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "General paediatrics. Singleton Hospital Child Health Department in Swansea was responsible for the care of over 6,000 acute admissions per year and a similar number of outpatient referrals. The department has lead consultants in all the mainstream paediatric sub-sections. My clinical duties included regular acute admissions, service weeks and out-of-hours on-call responsibilities. Until July 2009 I had an extensive outpatient practice throughout my consultant career. Many of my patients had significant neurodisability or other developmental problems and were seen by me throughout their childhood."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You also have an entry for diabetes and endocrinology, that might feature later, I'm not going to that right now. And it says this under neonatology:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Development of services for the newborn and the establishment of the Neonatal Intensive Care Centre for South-west Wales, lead consultant in neonatology 1980 to 1994, and shared neonatal duties with three consultant paediatricians until 2007."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And that unit provided facilities for a population of over 800,000 people. So to make it plain, I'm not disputing you have extensive experience, but it's not solely experience in neonatology; that's correct, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And your duties, even during that period, are shared with your duties as a consultant paediatrician?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And as you've said, a paediatrician will deal with the span of patients from babies through to the age of 16?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Would you agree that you will not therefore have the dayto-day exposure of someone who has been, for instance, a consultant neonatologist and solely a consultant neonatologist over a period of decades?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't really agree. I'll tell you why I don't agree.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We were where we were in the 1980s -- I'm not going to go on about this. Neonatology was a new discipline during the 1980s and, as I've said earlier, my generation were inspired to improve the services. We've heard how large a population we covered. You've also heard how few in number were the consultants compared to where we are these days everywhere.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Therefore, because there were so few consultants around, you had greater contact with -- we had contact with a greater number of babies than if you were, for instance, one of, I don't know, 10 neonatologists maybe.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore you dealt with all sorts of problems.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now, the other issue, which is quite important, from my -- as far as my neonatology development is this. My senior consultant, the other -- there were three of them during the 1980s and
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: 1990s, they deferred to my interest in neonatology in terms of developing services. Right?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: They deferred to my interest in terms of appointing staff and training staff.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore, my input into neonatology in terms of the babies I dealt with was huge. It did not -- and the other point that needs to be said, our on-call system was one in four. So in other words, I was on call every fourth weekend and every fourth weekday. And on top of that, we were, in the 1980s and 1990s, not only looking after neonates in Swansea, I was also looking after neonates in Neath. And the set up in Neath at that time was we only had a junior doctor, in other words the most junior GP trainee on the whole, and therefore when there were issues, you did not call a middle grade registrar, you called -- at weekends and so on, you called a consultant. And I can recall a number of occasions when I was called in because I was the only one really who could deal with this.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore, my hands-on experience of developing neonatal services from a clinical perspective, I am more than happy to say that it was as extensive as anybody's.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'm sorry, and on top of that I made sure that I attended neonatal courses. I remember going to the founding -- the initial meeting that Dr Peter Dunn, the Bristol neonatologist, one of my heroes, I remember going to a number of those meetings -- in fact the first one was when I was in Alder Hey, from memory, before I went to Swansea. So I carried on doing these neonatal course attendances, I visited Bristol on several occasions to top up my thoughts, et cetera, top up my knowledge.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore, it was full-on, let's make sure that we've got the best system going, best service going. Yes? So you can attach labels as long as you want, but in terms of my neonatology hands-on practice I am very, very comfortable with the expertise that I developed.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The other point in terms of hands-on expertise is this: I reckon I could intubate a baby today. It's one of these things, like riding a bicycle, that you don't forget how to do. Therefore I did quite a lot of hands-on stuff in terms of connecting ventilators, putting IV lines in, long lines in, umbilical catheters, all that sort of stuff, which I suspect in a bigger unit would be carried out by experienced junior doctors.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore I am very happy, Mr Myers, with my neonatology experience, expertise and background.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You described to us that the field of neonatology evolved during your clinical career.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It did, it has.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That follows, doesn't it, that therefore, if we consider the state of neonatology at the time we're looking at in this case, for a large part of your career your experience was not in that setting and of that type, was it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: From what I've seen from these cases and from 2015, I think the big changes occurred in the 1990s and the early part of this century. We've discussed in detail, correctly, things like monitoring, blood gas machines in units, that sort of thing. That's been around for over 20 years.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You told us you didn't use that Philips IntelliVue MP30 monitor, did you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You didn't use that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. I haven't seen it before today --
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- before yesterday.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So notwithstanding what you've said, that isn't something you used.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, no, there are different machines. That machine had a heart rate, an oxygen saturation and a respiratory rate monitor. We used, from memory, Hewlett Packard machines. It doesn't matter which make they are, but those monitors were in use in Swansea long -- you know, well, let's be blunt about it, I introduced them. I was the one who brought them in.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you work throughout your career in neonatology with all the types of equipment that we are going to be looking at, specifically that equipment that we're going to look at in this case?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Every one expect end-tidal CO2s. That's the little thing that you put to make sure that the CO2 changes colour. So that's a minor technical extension, a very important one, and they came in -- I can't remember when they came in, but I think they came in about 10 years ago. But every other principle in terms of ventilatory support that was in use in Chester in 2015, I was
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: familiar with all of them. I am familiar with all of them I should say.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Familiar in the day-to-day use of them?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Did you have a neonatal surgical unit attached to your hospital in Swansea.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, they went to Cardiff.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So in terms of working alongside neonatal surgeons and discussing matters with them day in, day out, you would not have done that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, we only discussed things with surgeons when we thought we needed a surgical opinion. The one thing we did do for a number of years is we held joint meetings between the paediatric surgeons in Cardiff and the paediatricians in Swansea, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You retired from clinical practice in 2009, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did from full-time clinical practice, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you were not working in neonatology over the period that we're dealing with in this case, 2015 to 2016, were you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Since retiring from clinical practice, a principal interest of yours has been in clinical negligence as an expert?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Is that correct? And also, particularly child protection?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Child safeguarding more than clinical negligence, really, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Child safeguarding?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Safeguarding, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: This case has involved you with a great deal of work in reviewing neonatology issues, hasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It has.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The bulk of your work in the years that you've been an expert has not been in neonatology?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: A lot of it has, actually. A lot of it has. A lot of my — for instance, my last clinical negligence case, which is fairly recent, is fairly recent, so yeah, so...
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If you get involved with, you know, the clinical negligence side, most of those -- most of the children I've dealt with were babies. So I've made absolutely sure that I've kept fully up to speed with neonatal practice and small baby practice. So quite happy with that.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Would you agree that the optimum position for someone dealing with expert evidence is to be in clinical practice at the time of making his or her report?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not necessarily. I think what's important is your clinical experience. I think if you look at doctors generally, you know, we have careers of 40 years or more and those careers evolve. You don't do the same job for 40 years. So therefore, during my career, as we have heard, I was the head of department and the clinical director, I was involved with setting up the baby unit, doing other things. So you develop your professionalism over -- throughout the whole of your career, which is fine. You do not spend the whole of your 40 years attached to an exclusive clinical scenario, you do not.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Medicine and medical practice changes constantly, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It does.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You described how it evolved in your career.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's important to be in clinical practice, so far as being an expert is concerned, because it enables you to find out more and develop your knowledge in the actual practice of your discipline, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And therefore if you're not in practice, you're at a disadvantage, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I am not at a disadvantage because one's experience is over such a long time and so extensive in the work that I did, you don't simply forget all of that the day you finish. In fact, you never forget it.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'm not suggesting you forget it, Dr Evans, but if you haven't been in practice at the time there is a new approach to things or people are dealing with it in a different way, you won't have experience of that, will you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If you care to tell me of any new approach with which I'm not familiar, I'd be happy to explore that. In terms of all the cases I have dealt with and the issues that occurred and the clinical issues that they presented with, babies do not change in terms of the illnesses they get over a period of 10 years. Babies have the same problems now that they had 100 years ago or more; it's simply that the way we deal with these problems changes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now, in terms of the basics of neonatology, the basic principles apply whether you're working in the 1980s or 2022. The basic principles remain the same.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The current recommendations for respiratory pressure for preterm babies, Dr Evans --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The current recommendation for respiratory pressure, resuscitation pressure, for preterm babies is in fact 25 centimetres, not 20 centimetres of water, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It varies, actually. It varies with the size of the baby. You saw that video where it said 30 centimetres of water and with prem babies it's 20 centimetres of water. This is where your clinical experience comes in: you have to deal with every patient on its merits.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That is what clinical practice is all about. And being pedantic about whether something is 25 or 30 doesn't get you anywhere if you're trying to be an effective clinician.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Small differences can make big differences with 20 babies(?), can't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely. Therefore when you're talking 20, 25 or 30, I'm sure that in my time I've used all of those pressures depending on the problem at hand.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Can I finally ask this on this topic: is it your view that not being in clinical practice makes no difference to the experience and knowledge you can bring to bear on what you're talking about?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. The difference is this: that if I am not in clinical practice -- I have not retired, I should remind everybody -- if I'm not in clinical practice I have time to explore other aspects of medicine or children's medicine, that is as important. I could for instance -- it would be very difficult for me to be here if I was a hands-on neonatologist working 5 days a week in Swansea or anywhere else. So therefore the experience I have accumulated over a long period of time has been crucial to my being able, in my opinion, to give you an objective and clear opinion on all of the cases that we are going to be discussing over the next few weeks and months.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Last topic I want to deal with this afternoon is this in terms of what your time is spent doing and what you do.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Since 2009, being an expert witness has in fact been your chief activity, hasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um... Yes, I suppose it has, actually, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Just looking at what you say in your statement about this, it's at page 4555, but I'm going to read it so we have this:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I have prepared reports relating to safeguarding issues for over 20 years and have given evidence in courts in civil cases in Wales, England, Ireland and Northern Ireland and in criminal cases in Wales and England. Between 2008 and August 2018 I have prepared over 220 reports relating to safeguarding issues at the request of the various participants. They include reports for courts (in excess of 70 cases), police authorities or the National Crime Agency (in excess of 60), solicitors for parents (in excess of 30), the defendant (in excess of 30), and the guardian and the local authority and the health board and the coroner."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Your focus has been on being an expert witness, hasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you've studied that, you've undergone the necessary training, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I have.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If I look at your CV at page 4, just so we can see, you have done training with Bond Solon --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- in 2017, 2019, 2020, 2021? Bond Solon offer training for people who are going to be giving evidence in courts; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I see 1 to 2 March 2018, you have attended a course at the Royal Society of Medicine, "Expert witness skills masterclass: how to avoid the pitfalls". The pitfalls of giving expert evidence does that mean?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, you know, how to make sure you present yourself properly, really.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You have expertise in writing reports?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I do.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And expertise in coming to court and giving evidence?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I do.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Would you agree with me if I suggest really that the main thing you are an expert in doing at the moment, Dr Evans, is being an expert?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What does that mean?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: As an expert witness.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think that's far too flash for me. I would say that I am here as a children's specialist with a huge experience of looking after small sick babies and I'm pleased -- and my role here is to assist the court in sorting out some extremely challenging issues. So I do not call myself -- you know, today, for instance, I have called myself an independent medical witness. I have not, from this, called myself an expert anything. So I call myself an independent medical witness and that and my opinion is based not on being an expert, my opinion is based on being a doctor. Okay?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We make no disagreement with the assessment that they are extremely challenging issues.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: My Lord, those are the questions that we ask at this stage.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I have no re-examination. Does your Lordship have any questions for Dr Evans at this stage?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: No, just one of clarification for the benefit of the jury. A few minutes ago it was put to you that when you were going through the various reports you prepared and who you've acted for, on whose instructions, that sort of thing, you referred to solicitors acting for parents, the defendant, the guardian. The local authority health board, the guardian, it's not the newspaper it's called a guardian ad litem, it's a person appointed by the court to represent the issues of the child.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That is correct, my Lord, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I should have clarified that, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: All right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. That completes your evidence at this stage. You'll be required to come back and you'll obviously be alerted as to when you are required to come back.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you very much at this stage.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Members of the jury, you'll remember I said we couldn't start until 11 o'clock on Monday. I remind you of that. It's not a rail strike day, I don't think, is it? No, it's not. Someone will tell me when the next one of those is and we'll address that if we get one on a court working day.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. That's it, the end of the week, the weekend is coming. My advice to you is -- of course, you can't put out of your mind entirely what role you are fulfilling in this very serious and very important case, but don't dwell on matters too much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: There's a long, long way to go, there's a lot of material to be placed before you for to you assess, so do other things, obviously, at the weekend and I'll see you, I hope, at 11 o'clock. If I'm a few minutes late, I apologise in advance. It will be my responsibility, but it's probably because something else has occurred that's impeded my movement. So 11 o'clock, please, be ready to start then. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And remember those vital instructions: no conversation by any means with anyone about anything to do with this case. No research about anyone or anything to do with this case. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: If you haven't already done it, I did it earlier this afternoon, plug your -- yes. Plug it in. As Mr Murphy said, he'll come around and do it all.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
Is your iPad plugged in? You've got it there, thank you very much. Thank you.
Just some confusion about what to do with some paperwork, I think. That's all it was.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's all right. Are both of you going down to see her?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, that will happen.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS
